bib.title: Delta Lake: High-Performance ACID Table Storage over Cloud Object Stores

question: How can ACID transactions and fast metadata operations be provided for large mutable tables stored on cloud object stores that are only eventually consistent key-value stores?
hypothesis: A transaction log stored in the object store itself (JSON records compacted into Parquet checkpoints) with optimistic concurrency is enough to give serializable ACID tables and much faster metadata operations, without a separate metadata service.
contributions: Delta Lake storage format: Parquet data objects plus a write-ahead log in _delta_log with checkpoints
Access protocols for serializable writes and snapshot-isolated reads over object stores, with per-store atomic commit
Higher-level features on the log: time travel, UPSERT/DELETE/MERGE, streaming ingest and tailing, OPTIMIZE and Z-ordering, caching, audit logging, schema evolution, connectors
Customer use cases and performance experiments

method.summary: Describes the Delta Lake design (Parquet objects plus an object-store-resident JSON log with Parquet checkpoints, optimistic concurrency via put-if-absent or rename or a coordinator) and reports four small benchmarks run by the authors' company: metadata cost vs partition count, Z-order skipping, TPC-DS power test and load time.

limits: Serializable transactions only within a single table (Sec 3.3, 7).
Commit rate limited to several transactions per second by object store write latency; millisecond streaming latency is hard, seconds achievable (Sec 3.4, 7).
No secondary indexes beyond min/max statistics; Bloom filter index only prototyped (Sec 7).

Benchmarks are vendor-run against an unnamed third-party Hive/Presto/Spark service, with no variance reported; the Hive/Presto gap in Fig 4 mixes Delta with Databricks Runtime optimizations (Parquet listing on Databricks Runtime took 450 s at 100,000 partitions).
Z-order experiment uses uniform random synthetic data; the 93% figure is an anecdotal customer result.

Z-order, SSD caching and auto optimize are Databricks service features; atomic commit on S3 needs a Databricks coordinator, while the open-source connector only serialises writers inside one SparkContext.
Dated: S3 LIST eventual consistency and no put-if-absent were 2020 facts; the Hudi and Iceberg comparison (Hudi one writer at a time) reflects 2020.

terms.definition: a directory on a cloud object store or file system that holds data objects with the table contents and a log of transaction operations (with occasional checkpoints)
set to false on add or remove actions that only rearrange existing data or add statistics, so streaming consumers can skip them
custom action with appId and version fields so applications can commit their own progress atomically with data, enabling exactly-once writes
a paradigm that combines the key features of data warehouses and data lakes: standard DBMS management functions usable directly against low-cost object stores

lineage.note: directories-of-files with Hive partition naming is the approach Delta replaces

lineage.work: Snowflake elastic data warehouse (Dageville et al.)
lineage.note: closed-world engine with a separate metadata service
concurrent work; one writer at a time per the paper
concurrent work lacking layout optimization and connectors to Redshift/Snowflake
metastore-based transactions, bottleneck at millions of partitions
